claims.text: A data-driven machine-learning model integrated with severe plastic deformation can simultaneously optimize phase stability, microstructure refinement, and material properties.
The target material is a coarse-grained, multiphase metallic or alloy system.
Such coarse-grained, multiphase systems are typically produced by conventional processing methods.
A machine-learning model can analyze processing data in real time to adjust severe-plastic-deformation and thermal parameters.
High-fidelity real-time data capture is feasible under significant thermomechanical loads in industrially relevant metallic systems.
Concurrent processing adjustments refine the grain structure.
Concurrent processing adjustments optimize the phase distribution.
The machine-learning algorithm can correlate processing parameters with microstructural evolution.
The machine-learning algorithm can correlate processing parameters with phase transformations.
These learned correlations enable in situ process optimization.
In situ process optimization enhances phase stability.
In situ process optimization improves material properties.
Machine-learning-guided severe plastic deformation improves phase stability relative to conventional thermomechanical processing.
Machine-learning-guided severe plastic deformation improves microstructure relative to conventional thermomechanical processing.
Machine-learning-guided severe plastic deformation improves mechanical properties relative to conventional thermomechanical processing.
Conventional thermomechanical processing uses isolated steps such as separate heat treatment and cold working that address individual properties.
The effectiveness of the proposed method depends on obtaining accurate real-time data and using a well-calibrated machine-learning model.
The magnitude of improvement may vary across alloy systems.
The magnitude of property enhancement and broad applicability require experimental validation.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is conventional thermomechanical processing with isolated heat-treatment and cold-working steps, whereas the experimental control is severe plastic deformation without machine-learning guidance. The falsification rule then refers to this control as conventional processing, leaving the actual comparator inconsistent.
